label: Toxic and Harmful Relationships
framing: Love is patient, but love is not a doormat, and Scripture never asks you to call harm by the name of devotion. If you are being abused, your safety comes first; in the United States you can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline any hour at 800-799-7233. Getting to safety is not a failure of faith but an act of it.
cultural: The ancient world gave the powerful nearly total reach over the weak, and the Bible quietly subverts it, protecting the vulnerable and warning against the friend whose kisses are deceitful. Jesus himself walked away from crowds that meant him harm and told his followers to shake the dust from their feet, never teaching that holiness means standing still to be destroyed.
historical: Scripture is honest about the wreckage of control, from Laban exploiting Jacob for twenty years to the men who used King David. The church has too often told victims to endure, and we must name that failure plainly; only in recent generations have pastors and counselors recovered what wisdom always knew, that protecting the harmed is the work of God, not a betrayal of the family.
application: If there is abuse, get safe before anything else, and tell someone who can help. Boundaries are not unforgiveness; they are the fence that makes love possible at a distance when it is not possible up close. Find a wise outside voice, a pastor or counselor who will not minimize what is happening, and do not let a misused verse keep you in harm's way.

verses.text: So Hagar gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: “You are the God who sees me,” for she said, “Here I have seen the One who sees me!”
verses.where: Hagar, an enslaved woman, is treated so harshly by Sarai that she runs into the desert while pregnant. Genesis tells the harm without approving it. God finds her there, and she names him the God who sees me. The angel's word that she should go back was spoken to one woman in one desert, and it is never a command for anyone today to return to someone who is hurting them.

verses.text: Saul tried to pin him to the wall with his spear. But the spear struck the wall and David eluded him, ran away, and escaped that night.
verses.where: King Saul, David's master and father-in-law, throws a spear at him again. David does not stay to prove his loyalty; he escapes that night, and his wife Michal helps him through a window. Leaving a person who is trying to harm you is not a failure of love or faith.

verses.text: For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God.
verses.where: David says he could have endured an enemy's insults. What breaks him is that the attack comes from a close friend, someone he walked with to the house of God. The Bible knows that the deepest harm often comes from people we trusted.

verses.text: His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart. His words are softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed.
verses.where: The same psalm describes the friend who broke his promises: his speech smooth as butter, his words softer than oil, while war is in his heart. Harmful people are often charming. Kind words do not cancel a pattern of harm.

verses.text: A hateful man disguises himself with his speech, but he lays up deceit in his heart. When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart.
verses.where: At the end of a chapter of portraits, Proverbs describes the hateful person who hides malice behind gracious speech, and says not to believe him when he speaks kindly. Wisdom learns to watch what a person does over time, not only what they say in the moment.

verses.text: Do not make friends with an angry man, and do not associate with a hot-tempered man, or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.
verses.where: From the sayings of the wise: do not make friends with a hot-tempered man, or you will learn his ways and be caught in a snare. Proverbs treats the people we keep close as one of the strongest forces shaping who we become.

verses.text: When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. Truly I tell you, you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.
verses.where: Jesus sends his disciples out as sheep among wolves and tells them to be shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves. When they are persecuted in one town, they are to flee to the next. He does not ask his followers to stay where they are being harmed in order to prove their faith.

verses.text: but Saul learned of their plot. Day and night they watched the city gates in order to kill him. One night, however, his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall.
verses.where: Soon after his conversion, Paul learns of a plot to kill him in Damascus, and other believers lower him in a basket through an opening in the city wall at night. The great apostle escaped danger with help from others, and Luke tells it without embarrassment.

verses.text: Jesus replied, “If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?”
verses.where: When an officer strikes Jesus during his questioning, Jesus does not strike back, and he does not stay silent either. He asks why he was struck. Refusing revenge is not the same as accepting mistreatment as right.

verses.text: The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked; His soul hates the lover of violence.
verses.where: David's friends urge him to flee, because the foundations seem to be crumbling. He answers by looking up: the LORD is on his throne, testing everyone, and his soul hates the lover of violence. God is not neutral about people who harm others.

verses.text: For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good, traitorous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these!
verses.where: Paul lists the marks of people who will trouble the church: self-loving, abusive, unloving, slanderous, brutal, treacherous, and yet keeping a form of godliness. His instruction to Timothy is plain: turn away from such people. Religious language does not make harm safe.

misread.taken: “Turn the other cheek” is used to tell people, often wives, children or church members, that a Christian must stay with someone who is hurting them and absorb it without complaint.
misread.says: Jesus is speaking of refusing revenge in matters of personal insult, not of accepting abuse. The examples he gives, a slap of insult, a lawsuit over a garment, a soldier forcing a mile of carrying, all concern personal wrongs and personal rights. When an officer struck Jesus, he asked why (John 18:23), and Paul used his rights under Roman law to stop a flogging (Acts 22:25). Seeking safety and the protection of the law is not disobedience to Jesus.
misread.text: But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also;

misread.taken: “Live at peace with everyone” is quoted to someone in a harmful relationship to mean that keeping the peace is their job, that leaving or speaking up is the sin, and that if things are not peaceful they have not tried hard enough.
misread.says: Paul writes “if it is possible” and “on your part” because he knows peace takes two. A believer must not be the one who refuses peace, but cannot always make it. The passage forbids revenge and calls for overcoming evil with good; it does not ask anyone to stay in danger or keep silent about harm. Leaving vengeance to God is not the same as leaving a person in harm's way.
misread.text: If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone.

whole: If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. Abuse is never the fault of the person who suffers it, and no verse in the Bible asks you to stay where you or your children are in danger.

Not every hard relationship is abusive, and not every abusive one looks it from outside. Some relationships wear a person down through control, contempt, threats, constant criticism, isolation from friends, or a pattern of harm followed by charm and apology. People in them often doubt their own judgment, wonder whether they are overreacting, and feel responsible for the other person's moods. Christians can feel trapped by words they were taught about forgiveness, submission, peace and the other cheek, as if faithfulness meant enduring anything.

The Bible does not teach that. It records harm honestly, from Sarai's treatment of Hagar to Saul's spear, and it does not call it good. It shows God seeing the one who was harmed. It shows faithful people fleeing danger, David through a window, Paul in a basket, the disciples from town to town at Jesus' own instruction. Its wisdom literature warns against people whose words are smooth while their hearts are at war, and Paul tells Timothy to turn away from those who are abusive even while they keep a form of godliness. Forgiveness in Scripture means giving up revenge and leaving judgment to God. It never means pretending harm is safe, and submission language must never be applied to abuse.

So the wisdom here begins with seeing clearly, which is often the hardest part, and then with not carrying it alone. Write down what has happened. Tell someone who will believe you. Where a crime has been committed, the police and the proper authorities are God's provision for protection, not a betrayal of the faith. Where a relationship is harmful but not dangerous, boundaries and wise counsel may help it change, or show that it cannot. And for anyone who has left, or is trying to, the God who saw Hagar in the desert sees you too.

differ.share: Christians agree that abuse is sin, that the one who suffers it is not to blame, that safety comes first, that churches must never cover abuse, and that crimes are to be reported to the authorities.

views.name: Separation, with limits on divorce
views.body: The Catholic Church teaches that a true sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved while both spouses live, but allows separation and can declare that a true marriage never existed. Some Protestant churches likewise permit separation for safety while limiting divorce and remarriage to adultery and desertion.

views.name: Abuse breaks the covenant
views.body: Many Protestant Christians count abuse as breaking the marriage covenant as surely as adultery or desertion, freeing the one who was harmed. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be for life but, as an act of mercy, allow a second marriage with a service of repentance.

differ.after: These differences concern divorce and remarriage. None of these churches teaches that anyone must stay in a home where they or their children are in danger. The Honest Answer “What does the Bible say about divorce and remarriage?” sets out the views at more length.

deep.sit: If a friend described your relationship to you in the same words you would use, what would you tell them to do?

prayer.lead: Psalm 55 was prayed by someone betrayed by a close companion. These verses are the turn: calling on God morning, noon and night, and being heard.
prayer.text: But I call to God, and the LORD saves me. Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice. He redeems my soul in peace from the battle waged against me, even though many oppose me.

careLines.text: If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first.
Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line.
If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true.
Tell someone you trust and get help.
What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault.
Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault.
These notes are not legal advice.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
